sources.headline: From Xinjiang to the Front Lines of Syria
sources.text:
In a dimly lit villa somewhere in the Idlib countryside, Choghtal, a slight, soft-spoken man, admitted that, back home, he had never held a gun. At 36, he is the second-in-command of the largest Uyghur militia in Syria. Growing up in Xinjiang, he was close to his par­ents and his sister; leaving them had never occurred to him. Then came the summer of 2009.
That June, a deadly brawl broke out at a toy factory in Guangdong province in southern China. The owners had brought in several hundred Uyghur workers; false rumors soon spread among the factory’s nearly 16,000 Han Chinese workers that the newcomers were ill-mannered, petty thieves, prone to violence—and that several of them had raped two Han women. This ignited a frenzy in which more than 120 people, most of them Uyghurs, were injured. The fighting ended only after two Uyghur men were bludgeoned to death.
Uyghur activists wrote open letters to top Chinese lead­ers asking for an investigation and began boycotting Guangdong products in protest, to no avail. On July 5, dozens of young Uyghurs on the opposite side of the country peacefully gathered in a square in Urumqi, Xinjiang’s capital, demanding a thorough state investigation into the deaths. Many Uyghurs felt that decades of systematic marginalization had fostered a lack of accountability whenever their people were concerned.
Police tried to disperse the students, which sparked a Uyghur rampage against police and Han civilians in Urumqi, insti­gating a cycle of violence between both eth­nic groups that lasted for days. The Chinese government said that 192 people were killed—about two-thirds of them Han—with more than 1,000 people injured. Rights groups have cast doubt on the official death toll.
Uyghur organizations say thousands of Uyghurs, mostly young men, were detained by state security forces and disappeared in the aftermath, though an actual fig­ure is unknown. For the next 10 months, regional authorities ramped up surveillance of Uyghurs, fortified checkpoints, and restricted internet access across Xinjiang.
Choghtal watched videos from his friends in Urumqi—of Chinese police crack­ing down on student demonstrators and of Han and Uyghur lynch mobs later prowling the streets—and discovered a well of cold fury inside him. He had seen hundreds of his own people peacefully take to the streets. He had seen people who looked like him try to stand up for themselves, only to be disappeared. If he stayed in Xinjiang, he felt that only prison or an early death awaited him. He began looking for ways to smug­gle himself out of the country.
Four years later, he found his opportunity. Choghtal snuck across the Chinese border and flew to Turkey. He left without telling his family, unable to face his sister’s sorrow. Choghtal vowed to continue his studies in Turkey and become a doctor. With an education, and by building influence among the Uyghur diaspora, perhaps he could help his fellow Uyghurs back home.
Choghtal began contemplating how the Uyghurs could study China’s own methods in Xinjiang and turn them against the Chinese state. He had to admit a begrudging respect for the Chinese government. “Yes, the regime is our enemy,” he said. “But they did not subjugate East Turkestan in one day; they did it step by step, with strategy and methodical tactics.”
In dozens of hours of interviews, Uyghur fighters and their families were unanimous on one point: They felt that decades of political and cultural repression by the Chinese Communist Party had given them no option but to take up arms. “I never decided to leave East Turkestan,” Choghtal said. “They forced me to leave. They drove us out.”
A photograph of a group of tribesmen clear rubble from their destroyed houses following Pakistan military airstrikes against suspected Taliban hideouts in Miranshah in North Waziristan on May 24, 2014.
Tribesmen clear rubble from their destroyed houses following Pakistani military airstrikes against suspected Taliban hideouts in Miranshah in North Waziristan on May 24, 2014.Thir Khan/AFP via Getty Images
The search for a temporary Uyghur homeland outside Chinese control began as early as the late 1990s. Aspiring Uyghur fighters needed a place that was not too picky about passports and residency documents that would give them space to create a community free of Chinese surveillance. Ideally, such a place would also teach them how to organize politically and train militarily.
Uyghurs in Xinjiang first looked to countries on their borders, where Islamist militant movements such as al Qaeda, the Taliban, and the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan already existed. Abdukerim, a serial entrepreneur who left Xinjiang in 2011, said he first made his way to Waziristan, a remote mountainous region in Pakistan dominated by powerful tribes. He and about a dozen other Uyghur fighters moved from tribe to tribe along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, looking for a militant group that could train them.
They did not have much luck and found conditions inhospitable. The global war on terror was starting to wind down, but Abdukerim and two other Uyghurs who also cycled through Afghanistan and Pakistan during this time described constant U.S. drone surveillance overhead and frequent aerial strikes and bombings. The border was nearly impossible to traverse on foot or by car, and the lack of medical facilities meant fighters who were injured had no place for treatment.
The ideology of the Uzbekistan Islamists and the Taliban was also off-putting to many Uyghurs, who had grown up with the Sufi-inflected forms of Sunni Islam more commonly practiced in Xinjiang. “Their ideology was almost akin to that of ISIS,” said Moaz, 55, a Uyghur fighter who also ended up in Waziristan during this time.
Moaz recalled that the Uzbeks were overwhelmingly focused on establishing a religious caliphate, expelling U.S. forces—toward whom he felt no personal antipathy—from the region, and confronting Israel, an issue he felt also “had nothing to do with” the Uyghurs.
The Uzbek militants he initially lived with also believed it was morally acceptable to kill civilians in war zones, a religious position Moaz considered “cruel behavior.” He kept his objections to himself, however, because he relied on the Uzbeks to ferry him across borders to his intended destination: Syria, where he had heard Uyghur communities were already forming.
In 2012, Abdukerim and about 20 other Uyghurs decided to leave Afghanistan for Syria, where civil war was underway. “We wanted to train in the real world,” he said.
The Uyghurs of Syria effectively formed their own organization, hived off from their predecessors in Afghanistan, with their own political strat­egies and aims. Most of the Uyghurs in Syria belonged to a group called the Turkestan Islamic Party, but at least a few dozen fighters belonged to two other, much smaller organizations, and all three worked frequently together, often with doz­ens of other militias and rebel groups, throughout the Syrian civil war.
The Syrian Uyghurs were intentionally non­aligned. And even though an undeniably fundamentalist reli­giosity structured their community, they leaned toward nationalist, rather than ideological, goals. They sought to create their own state, in their own homeland—not a caliphate, but a nation.
In 2013, Choghtal crossed from Turkey into northern Syria with little but the clothes on his back. There, he glimpsed an alternative future for his people, one in which they were not enfeebled, perpetual victims. He had tried to avoid taking up arms, but decided to resist no longer. A few days later, he began military training.
Over the next three months, he and a few dozen other recruits would go through a rigorous regimen designed by Syrian and Uyghur militant fighters in the Idlib countryside. The Uyghurs who came to Syria had virtually no fighting experience. They had been teachers, farmers, writers, truck drivers, civil engineers, and small-time traders who had sold things like textiles and shoes back in Xinjiang.
“When the first bombs fell down on us, I was so scared. I wanted to hide, but I did not know where to hide,” Bilal, a former hairdresser, said. “But after a while I learned you can guess how far away a bomb is and how long it will take to make contact, based on the pitch and audio profile of the whistle as it comes down.”
A photograph shows the explosion high above the northern Syrian city of Kobani during a suicide car bomb attack by the Islamic State group (ISIS) seen from the outskirts of Suruc, on the Turkey-Syria border, Oct. 20, 2014.
A plume of smoke rises above the northern Syrian city of Kobani following a suicide car bomb attack by the Islamic State, seen from the outskirts of Suruc, on the Turkey-Syria border, on Oct. 20, 2014.Gokhan Sahin/Getty Images
Despite fighting a foreign war in a foreign land, often communicating in a foreign tongue with other Islamist groups, the Uyghurs learned quickly and leveraged themselves into strategic positions in northern Syria. Through cunning and force of will, they refashioned a motley assemblage of volunteers into seasoned soldiers, learning quickly in the middle of an active war zone, where the cost of failure was death.
On a dry, windswept hill in northern Syria, those costs are evident: There stands a cemetery filled with white stone markers, one for each Uyghur fighter killed in the civil war. “No one wants to die in a foreign land, so far from home,” said Anas, a fighter who ran his own transport company in Xinjiang. “But we feel proud they sacrificed their own lives to liberate this land. One day, somebody will write about them, and it will encourage our nation’s people to live courageously.”
A photograph shows a lone Al Qaeda affiliated Turkestan Islamic Party fighter as he fires a rocket at Syrian Army positions near Abu Duhur Airbase in the Idlib Governorate, Syria on Jan. 13, 2018.
An al Qaeda-affiliated Turkestan Islamic Party fighter fires a rocket at Syrian army positions near Abu al-Duhur Air Base in Idlib, Syria, on Jan. 13, 2018.ZUMA Press Wire/Reuters
By 2014, a serious threat against the Uyghur cause was emerging: the Islamic State. The Islamic State and its affiliate in Afghanistan had been trying to recruit Uyghurs for years, using Islamist language of global jihad to entice foreign fighters eager for action. But most Uyghurs in Syria were unhappy with the Islamic State’s recruiting efforts. They had come to Syria to learn how to build a Uyghur state, not an Islamic caliphate.
There were religious differences as well as ideological ones: Even devout Uyghurs felt the Islamic State was too fundamentalist.
“I saw how they terrorize people and kill civilians. That’s not acceptable,” said Abdallah, a Uyghur fighter in his late 30s. “They sold this story about how they would help Uyghurs and use Islam to create a free and prosperous world, and because some Uyghurs believed them, they were sacrificed needlessly.” Especially controversial was the fact that the Islamic State would kill fellow Muslims.
The disagreements over the Islamic State prompted intense, sometimes violent schisms among the Uyghurs’ ranks. During one hair-raising standoff in 2016, an Islamic State-affiliated group tried to declare a caliphate in rural northern Idlib. About 70 Uyghurs decided to join. When Jabhat al-Nusra, one of the Uyghurs’ main Syrian allies among the rebel groups, moved to storm the caliphate, an Islamic State commander threatened to detonate a suicide vest. A Jabhat fighter shot him dead.
As Jabhat al-Nusra intensified its fight against the Islamic State, it also arrested suspected collaborationist Uyghurs. A few Islamic State fighters made it back to the Uyghur commu­nities in Idlib, but the rifts between family and friends did not heal. “Some of them called their own family infidels,” recalled Ahmad Ziad, a Uyghur religion teacher. “They would say to their own family, ‘I have a bullet waiting for you.’”

sources.headline: The Uyghurs Who Fought in Syria’s Civil War
sources.text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Emily Feng – author of “Our Hearts Burned for Home: Uyghur Militants in Syria’s Civil War” (Columbia Global Reports 2026) and award-winning correspondent for NPR – is the 530th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
What was the impetus behind your reporting on Uyghur militants in Syria’s civil war?
For years, I had been reporting on the ground on the Xinjiang region and the sweeping detention campaign that began in early 2017. And one of the reasons cited in rare official comments from Beijing about why authorities were detaining and arresting hundreds of thousands Uyghur people mentioned the presence of Uyghur “terrorists” in Syria and Afghanistan, but offered no evidence and since these places were nearly impossible to access, no one had done interviews with any of these supposed Uyghur militants.
In late 2024, it suddenly became possible to go to Syria after the surprising collapse of the Assad regime there and the end of a terrible civil war. Coincidentally, I was in nearby Lebanon when the Assads fled to Russia, and I ended up spending much of the beginning of 2025 in Syria.
Imagine my surprise when I saw Uyghur fighters milling about Syria! Indeed, there were thousands of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and I was later to discover, their role in the civil war had been much more impactful than anyone expected.
But I sensed there was much more to the story about these Uyghur fighters than Beijing’s narrative – that these were masterminds behind fatal attacks on Chinese civilians who were now hellbent on destroying China. I wondered what had made them leave their families and livelihoods behind to live in an active war zone, and how they had transformed themselves from hairdressers and engineers and teachers into hardened militant fighters, working in alliance with Arabic-speaking, Syrian rebel groups.
I was also sensitive to the possible implications of reporting on Uyghurs. In no way is their existence in Syria justification for the detention and arrests, mostly without real due process, of so many Uyghur citizens of China. I resolved to find a way to contact the Syrian Uyghurs and interview them – a difficult task, as they had operated as a secretive and highly-disciplined force for more than a decade – and learn more about why they had come to the Middle East.
Analyze the factors propelling Uyghur militants to join the civil war and how they contributed to the overthrow of the Assad regime.
I don’t want to give too much away here! The details are in the book. But in short, many Uyghurs who ended up in Syria had initially hoped to put down roots in Turkey, where a sizeable Uyghur diaspora already exists. However, Turkey does not want these Uyghurs, and it has stymied their ability to get residence documents and even aided in their deportation back to China.
Turkey happens to share a long, mostly unfortified border with northern Syria, however, where a rebel-held swath of territory had been established in a growing civil war. And so that’s where a lot of Uyghurs headed, because Syria was not checking documents or asking for visas, frankly. All of them were also looking for a constructive way to help Uyghurs back in Xinjiang, or East Turkestan as the Uyghurs call it, and they hoped Syria would become a base to fight back politically or militarily against the Chinese Communist Party.
A good number of Uyghurs had also already heard of the possibility of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and they were eager to train militarily. An active war, one Uyghur commander later told me, was free practice.
The Uyghurs’ wholehearted embrace of violence for the sake of establishing an independent Uyghur state is controversial, I should mention, among the Uyghur diaspora globally. But of the five dozen or so interviews I did with Uyghur fighters and their families, all of them described experiences where they felt diplomacy or political activism had failed them, and they felt they had nothing left to lose anymore by taking up arms.
The deadly race riots that began July 5, 2009 in Urumqi, which left scores of both Han Chinese and Uyghur Chinese dead, was a real turning point for many Uyghurs I met. The mob violence they witnessed from all parties that week and the ensuing crackdown and racism Uyghurs experienced in the aftermath convinced the majority of the fighters I spoke to to seek their fortunes in Turkey and later Syria.
What surprised me the most after weeks on the ground in Syria with Uyghur fighters was discovering the reach and breadth of the Uyghurs’ role in the Syrian civil war. The participated in major battles, played a key role in helping rebels with Hayat Tahrir Al-Sham (HTS) take Aleppo, and eventually marched into Damascus to establish the new government. HTS’ Ahmed Al Sharaa, now Syria’s president, privately credits the Uyghurs with being a consistently loyal, effective fighting force, and for that reason, the Uyghurs now have an unusual political purchase in the new Syria.
Explain the difference between the Turkestan Islamic Party (TIP) and East Turkmenistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and how China views their respective identities.
Both of these entities are part of a broader movement of Uyghurs who have taken up arms and seek to establish an independent Uyghur homeland in the Xinjiang region. I found evidence that members of both groups still maintain communication links, and some of the earliest TIP fighters in Syria initially tried to train with ETIM officials along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
But to call ETIM in particular an organization would be a stretch, based on what I was able to find. The ETIM-linked fighters I met said there were never many Uyghurs along the Af-Pak border, many were killed in American bombings, training was nearly impossible due to the difficult geography of the place, and there were ideological differences between the more relaxed Uyghurs and the more conservative al-Qaida-linked and Taliban fighters there.
TIP, the Syria branch of this nationalist Uyghur militant movement, was much more successful. They became highly disciplined and managed to remain organized, sharing scarce financial resources in self-sustaining communities in Idlib, in northern Syria, and setting up robust social services for a growing Uyghur population that has now reached 20,000 men, women, and children.
While TIP also maintained substantial links to al-Qaida affiliated groups, including with HTS, for years, these links later became problematic and internally divisive as TIP and HTS tried to brand themselves as politically more mainstream and welcoming to Syrians and Uyghurs of all castes. Yet TIP remains controversial within Syria, and also within much of the Uyghur diaspora community, who view their militant past with distaste.
Why are Uyghur militants controversial in Syria?
The Syria Uyghurs find themselves in an awkward position. At home, they were the oppressed. In Syria, they are widely viewed as oppressors, in the eyes of Syria’s many minority communities.
Foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, are viewed with fear and suspicion, as the civil war quickly devolved into a proxy war for various nation states and Islamist groups. Many remain in Syria in peacetime, creating resentments among Syrians who wish for the foreigners to return to their home countries. All the time, Uyghurs are confused with Uzbek fighters, and so many Syrians also do not know why the Uyghurs came to Syria in the first place, and do not understand why they cannot simply return to China.
During the civil war, the Sunni Uyghurs were active in besieging Shiite Syrian villages. They were frequently attacked by Hezbollah proxy forces and retaliated against Shiite populations in response. And for many years, the Uyghurs occupied and lived in several Shiite and Christian villages whose residents had fled in advance of Sunni Islamist groups like TIP arriving, which sowed more distrust and fear among Syrian minority communities who are increasingly on edge under the Sunni HTS-dominated government in Damascus. The Uyghurs maintain they are friendly neighbors and open to Syrians of other faiths and have tried to moderate their religious beliefs somewhat, but there are often significant cultural and linguistic gaps between them and Syrians, which the Uyghurs themselves sometimes do not even fully grasp.
Finally, there were also reports that the Uyghurs were among the perpetrators, alongside Syrian government soldiers, of horrific massacres of mostly Alawi Syrians in 2025. I found no evidence to suggest Uyghurs were involved, and they have no interest in doing so, as involvement would certainly imperil their still uncertain and vulnerable status as stateless refugees in Syria.
Assess the role of Uyghur militants in China-Syria relations and the implications for China-U.S. relations.
In some ways, the Uyghurs are not very important to China-Syria, or broader China-Middle East, relations. Syria has made it clear that it will not let groups on its soil threaten China, even though they also have made it clear they will not send the Uyghurs to China, as Beijing has demanded.
For China however, the Uyghurs are the top issue for them in Syria, and successive diplomatic delegations to Damascus have always mentioned TIP and the Uyghurs as the dominant concern Beijing has for the new government.
The result is that Gulf states, notable Saudi Arabia, have become major investors in Syria’s post-war reconstruction. China was once one of Syria’s top economic partners before the civil war, and it does not look like it will regain that position.
It will be interesting to see how the Uyghurs navigate their future in Syria. Will they buy land and build houses — setting up a much more permanent community in Syria? Will their children born in Syria still maintain strong Uyghur identity links and a commitment to set up a Uyghur state, when they feel more and more wedded to their Syrian upbringing as the years go by?

sources.headline: How Taiwan Activates Beijing’s Chosen Fear
sources.text: The standard explanations for why Taiwan is so important to the Chinese Communist Party are familiar: territorial integrity, credibility of deterrence commitments, great power competition with the United States, the strategic value of the first island chain, and the semiconductor industry concentrated in TSMC’s fabrication facilities. These explanations work, but they don’t tell the whole story. Rational strategic calculation does not produce a posture in which a nuclear-armed state with the world’s second-largest economy treats a democratic island of 23 million people as a permanent, non-negotiable crisis. But what is rational depends largely on how history has defined you and the ways in which you have defined yourself.The Chinese Communist Party’s posture toward Taiwan is driven not primarily by strategic calculation, at least not in the way it is understood from outside. Its posture is driven by a political trauma the party has consistently chosen to adopt and emphasize: three millennia of Chinese political history, interpreted through what I call the fragmentation pattern. This describes the situation in which a displaced regime establishes a rival power node that continues to claim sovereignty over the whole. It then either reconquers the center or is destroyed. The fact that this binary is false is irrelevant: It is the story that has been embraced, and cynically cultivated.Beijing is finding that echoed civilizational trauma invoked in the name of regime stability is not easily discarded. The resulting ways in which the party is obliged to act are shaped by this narrative. For the United States, the consequence is significant: Deterrence built around imposing costs may fail if Beijing perceives inaction itself as a threat to regime survival. Understanding the historical template through which the Chinese Communist Party interprets Taiwan is therefore necessary to understanding what will deter Beijing and where U.S. strategy is most likely to miscalculate.China’s Political Trauma: Experienced and EngineeredVictoria Tin-bor Hui’s comparative analysis of Chinese and European state formation argues that neither Chinese unification nor European fragmentation was structurally inevitable: Both were the products of strategic choices, particularly the self-strengthening reforms that allowed dominant states to absorb rivals. She argues specifically against geographic determinism in favor of political agency: The Chinese heartland was just as prone to political fragmentation as any other region. There was no foreordained pattern. China was never destined to be a centrally controlled single state. The fact that it happened repeatedly has no intrinsic value, but tremendous propaganda worth to anyone wishing to point to a tradition of political unity. The patterns of history may not themselves be deterministic, but they are politically useful, and the Chinese motif of unification has proved extraordinarily useful to the Chinese Communist Party.Fragmentation and reunification have been the defining rhythm of Chinese political life, and a generation of Chinese citizens — including today’s cadres — have been schooled in it the way American officers are schooled in the lessons of Pearl Harbor and the Cuban Missile Crisis. On both counts the events themselves were real and documented, but American education focuses on the events as a product of their time and geopolitical circumstance, not a historical motif. Mark Edward Lewis’s histories of the early Chinese empires document the cycle from its origins: the Warring States period that preceded Qin unification in 221 B.C. and the collapse of the Han into the Three Kingdoms. The pattern repeated through the Sui, the Tang, the Song partition, and the Yuan Mongol conquest. The Ming expelled the Mongol Yuan, reunified China, then fell to the Manchu Qing. Southern Ming loyalist courts persisted for nearly two decades claiming continued legitimate authority over all of their former empire. The Qing collapse in 1912 produced warlordism, civil war, and left China vulnerable to Japanese invasion.The lesson that the modern Chinese Communist Party has chosen to learn, and rely on, is this: When a Chinese dynasty falls, the displaced regime or its successors do not accept the loss and establish an independent state. They relocate, claim continued sovereignty over the whole, and persist as a standing challenge to the legitimacy of whoever holds the center. The Eastern Jin fled south after the fall of the Western Jin and ruled from Nanjing for over a century while non-Chinese dynasties held the north. The Southern Ming established rival courts after the Manchu conquest and fought on for nearly 20 years. The conclusion that can be drawn if only considering these cases is that the rival claimant represented an existential challenge to the legitimacy of the ruling dynasty, and the dynasty that tolerated the rival claimant’s existence was eventually judged to have failed the fundamental test of governance.That test has a name that is so familiar it has become a cliché, which is precisely why its operational significance is underestimated: the Mandate of Heaven. The concept, which dates to the early Zhou dynasty, is not divine-right doctrine in the European sense. It is much better understood as a performance standard. Dingxin Zhao traces how the Western Han fused Confucian moral legitimation and Legalist administrative control, with the mandate as the test of that system: The ruler held it as long as he governed competently, maintained order, and preserved the unity of the realm. The mandate’s withdrawal is demonstrated by natural disasters, popular unrest, and above all by the fracture of political unity — when the ruler morally fails.The existence of a rival claimant is, then, evidence that the mandate is in doubt and represents a direct refutation of the regime’s legitimacy. It is part of the evaluative framework through which political legitimacy has been assessed far beyond living memory, and it is the framework that Beijing has chosen to evaluate itself by. Zheng Wang’s research on Chinese political memory shows how the party maintains this framework through its schools. The patriotic education campaign launched after 1989 made the choice of which history to remember, putting the Century of Humiliation and the equation of national unity with national survival at the center of Chinese identity. Wang, borrowing the psychiatrist Vamik Volkan’s term, calls this a chosen trauma. The template is not merely inherited but actively reinforced by the state. This reinforcement only further constrains Beijing on the Taiwan question. To back down becomes a blow to legitimacy out of all proportion to its actual significance.Taiwan fits the pattern Beijing has chosen to embrace with a precision that should alarm anyone responsible for deterrence planning in the Western Pacific. In 1949, the Chinese Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan after losing the civil war to Chairman Mao Zedong’s Communist forces. They did not establish an independent state. They established the Republic of China on Taiwan and maintained, for decades, that they were the legitimate government of all of China. The Nationalists occupied China’s seat at the United Nations until 1971. They maintained a posture of eventual reconquest well into the Cold War. The rival claim has softened over time as Taiwan democratized and developed its own identity, but the structural fact remains: A defeated regime retreated to a nearby position, claimed sovereign authority, and has persisted for 77 years under foreign protection.All of this tells a very neat story, and it’s the story that the Chinese Communist Party has been telling for decades. But the Century of Humiliation narrative, stretching from the Opium Wars through the Japanese invasion to the Communist victory, is less historical analysis than political engineering. Rana Mitter shows how the narrative of Chinese experiences in World War II was deliberately constructed to prime the threat architecture of the Chinese population for a specific emotional payload: the memory of foreign exploitation and civilizational degradation, with the Chinese Communist Party positioned as the sole agent of restoration. General Secretary Xi Jinping’s “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” is both a slogan and a commitment — framed in the language of the mandate — that the Chinese Communist Party will complete the civilizational task that every previous dynasty was measured by. Taiwan’s continued separation is, within this framework, proof that the task is unfinished.The Chinese Communist Party’s narrative seems to have survived its own historical counterexamples. The Northern Song Dynasty coexisted with its Liao neighbors after decades of warfare. Under the 1005 Treaty of Chanyuan, it accepted the Liao ruler as an equal emperor. The Eastern Jin, which the party’s reading treats as a rival claimant, opened a multi-state era: From A.D. 317 to 589, through the Northern and Southern Dynasties, China functioned as a system of rival states for over 250 years. The Yuan court, as the Northern Yuan, resisted every Ming attempt to extinguish it in Mongolian exile. These historical episodes seem to call into question the truism that a rival claimant continuing to maintain total sovereignty is fundamentally intolerable. Yet the Chinese Communist Party, having fully committed itself to the pattern, cannot accept the record of history it did not choose.Treating rival claimants for sovereignty, breakaway territories, and every other flavor of territorial dispute as an existential problem is not a trait limited to the Chinese Communist Party. North and South Korea technically remain in a state of war and both governments treat that fact as a critical reality, yet peace has largely been maintained on the peninsula for seventy years. Time has decoupled reunification from regime survival. Russia has shown repeatedly its willingness to use military force against its neighbors for various reasons, all framed as existential. They are existential: just to Vladimir Putin, not to the Russian state. What sets apart the Chinese pattern is the deep pedigree of the falsehood. China can rightly claim to have a linguistic and civilizational record that stretches back millennia, and this is exactly what the Chinese Communist Party has tried to tap into. In doing so it has solidified its control over a staggering amount of territory and people, but it has also tied itself to an outdated template it found useful to cultivate and did so in such a way that it cannot be easily abandoned by the regime.A choice hardens into a constraint once it is written into institutions, and this one has been written everywhere. The 2005 Anti-Secession Law put the claim into statute. The 2023 Patriotic Education Law makes reunification a mandatory subject of state education and calls completing it a “sacred duty” of all Chinese, Taiwanese included. A 2022 white paper declared reunification indispensable to national rejuvenation — Xi’s signature slogan. In 2013 Xi told a Taiwanese envoy the problem could not be passed down from one generation to the next, which constitutes a sharp break from Deng Xiaoping’s willingness to wait a thousand years. Each layer raises the price of walking away, however contingent the origins. After three decades of reinforcement, reunification is more tightly bound to regime survival in Beijing than when the campaign began.Those bonds do, however, have some slack. sources.headline: How China and America Can Move from Competition to Stability
sources.text: The American team thought it was signaling restraint. The Chinese team saw preparations for combat. In a closed-door Sino-American crisis simulation I helped organize in the 2010s — which the U.S. military funded as part of a long-term project — the Americans repositioned an aircraft carrier away from a maritime dispute between China and the Philippines, expecting the move to reassure Beijing. Instead, the Chinese participants became deeply alarmed. They believed the carrier was now ideally positioned to launch combat operations while remaining less vulnerable to attack. The episode revealed how suspicion could turn an intended reassurance into an apparent threat. This danger becomes more intense when each side views the other primarily through the lens of strategic competition.For nearly a decade, strategic competition has framed the U.S. approach to China, shaping military planning and operations, alliance diplomacy, trade and technology relations, investment policy, and — increasingly — scientific, educational, and cultural exchanges.While strengthening deterrence and inspiring improvements in America’s competitive capabilities, strategic competition has become an end in itself, encouraging dangerous policies often based on rigid, worst-case assumptions about Chinese intentions and abilities. And the same dynamic operates on the Chinese side. The framework fails to answer a central question: What kind of stable and beneficial U.S.-Chinese relationship is such competition intended to produce?Both sides require greater reassurance, positive incentives to exercise restraint and cooperation, and recognition of the need for an enduring, stable balance supported by substantive, lasting agreements. Without these, stress on strategic competition is likely to produce recurring crises, accelerating arms competition, economic and technological fragmentation, and even a full-scale war, potentially involving nuclear weapons and most likely over Taiwan. Even without such a catastrophic outcome, strategic competition will almost certainly diminish cooperation on potentially existential, global threats such as climate change and the disruptive effects of emerging technologies like AI.The 2026 National Defense Strategy states that the United States does not seek to “dominate,” “strangle,” or “humiliate” China. It also describes the American objective as an Indo-Pacific balance of power that allows a “decent peace,” and stresses homeland and Western Hemisphere security. It also does not mention Taiwan, a major potential source of conflict. Such wording suggests the Trump administration is moving away from intense strategic competition backed by American superiority.And yet, the same document calls for a strong denial defense against China along the first island chain extending from the Korean Peninsula to Southeast Asia, as well as an overall “favorable balance of power” in the Asia-Pacific, implying a continued need to geographically contain China through superior military power, as opposed to a stable balance based on mutual denial capabilities. The strategy does not offer reciprocal political limits or an agreed end-state for the relationship. And U.S. force modernization, alliance cooperation, and technology restrictions remain heavily shaped by concerns about a threatening China.Despite the positive rhetoric occurring in parts of the National Defense Strategy and during both of this year’s meetings between President Donald Trump and General Secretary Xi Jinping, U.S. policy remains a largely zero-sum competitive struggle requiring clearly superior, if not entirely dominant, military power to contain or constrain Beijing. The emphasis remains on “winning” a competition over creating a stable, beneficial outcome. As a result, the relationship still lacks an operational political framework for the “decent peace” called for by the United States.Washington should pursue a strategy that bounds bilateral competition within a relationship that protects both countries’ vital interests while reducing conflict risks and expanding opportunities for positive-sum outcomes. This process is best described by the Chinese concept endorsed by both leaders during the Beijing summit: constructive strategic stability. In an attempt to define this concept, Beijing has articulated broad principles and both governments have announced specific cooperative initiatives, but neither has publicly set out a coherent, sequenced framework linking specific political assurances to verifiable reciprocal restraint measures and, ultimately, durable agreements.The Illogic and the Limits of Strategic CompetitionThere are many reasons why a policy of strategic competition does not serve American (or Chinese) interests.First, it offers no clear, stable, mutually beneficial political end-state. Instead, the United States largely measures success through stronger military deployments, tighter anti-China alliances, export and investment controls, tariffs, and other restrictions. Under this approach, competition becomes self-reinforcing, as Chinese trade and technological gains invite additional restrictions, military modernization justifies larger deployments and increased defense spending, and diplomatic or political advances prompt zero-sum counters. Much the same set of responses is seen on the Chinese side.Second, as a result, this approach encourages both sides to securitize nearly every aspect of the relationship, from trade and technology to scientific exchanges. As a result, an increasing number of activities by either side become subject to intense restrictions or prohibitions for real and imagined “national security” reasons.Third, this dynamic deepens mistrust and encourages worst-case planning. The trajectory points toward either a competition for predominance or an unstable balance in which both sides constantly seek leverage, increasing the danger of military confrontation and conflict. In such an environment, procedural “guardrails” will prove insufficient unless the two governments also reach substantive, reciprocal arrangements that reduce the underlying sources of conflict.Fourth, while any lasting strategy requires realistic assessments of each side’s capabilities, strategic competition encourages inflated views of both the challenges each side poses and each side’s ability to counter them, producing unrealistic expectations.China is a formidable economic, technological, and military power and at times uses its capabilities to counter U.S. interests, including by restricting critical-mineral exports to the United States and, according to U.S. intelligence and cybersecurity agencies, penetrating U.S. critical-infrastructure networks to prepare for disruption during a crisis or conflict. It also undermines U.S. interests by supporting both Russia and Iran with military and dual-use components in their respective conflicts with Ukraine and the United States. But such actions do not justify portraying Beijing as an existential threat in other than nuclear warfare terms, or assuming its growth and influence in every case come at America’s expense, necessitating a U.S. drive for dominance or clear superiority and zero-sum pushback on every front.Despite efforts to reduce its vulnerability to outside pressure and its desire to stress state sovereignty and collective rights over liberal democratic ideas, China remains deeply integrated into the international economy, from which it has benefited and to which it has contributed significantly. Moreover, China faces structural constraints on its ability to achieve global normative and power dominance, such as adverse demographics, high debt and property sector weakness, and slowing productivity and growth. It also suffers under ideological constraints and a political system with limited international appeal.While posing a military challenge to U.S. maritime predominance in the Western Pacific that requires sustained balancing, Beijing is highly unlikely to be able to assemble the capabilities needed for global military dominance in the foreseeable future — if ever — including extensive alliances, overseas bases, worldwide logistics, and broad international acceptance of Chinese leadership.For its part, the United States is constrained in sustaining its historical predominance by steadily growing fiscal pressures, political polarization, public resistance to military escalation and prolonged wars (evident in polling on Iran), less-compliant allies, and a broader diffusion of global power.Finally, open-ended strategic competition distorts American priorities and damages prosperity and long-term strength. The administration’s budget proposals prioritize defense spending while reducing overall funding for civilian programs, weakening investment in the domestic foundations of competitiveness and national well-being.The Alternative: What Constructive Strategic Stability Means and Where It Came FromIn rejecting strategic competition, America should not return to engagement and hedging. While producing decades of relative stability, mutually beneficial economic interaction, and normalized exchanges, that policy downplayed unavoidable competition and became associated with unrealistic expectations of Chinese political liberalization and near-complete acceptance of the U.S.-led international system. Alhough hedging was arguably a logical form of insurance against a more aggressive China, Washington never fully defined, delimited, and implemented the concept. Moreover, as with strategic competition, neither notion defined a sustainable end-state for the relationship.The term “strategic stability” has its roots in Cold War efforts to limit the dangers of U.S.-Soviet nuclear competition. Its current usage is much broader, however, referring to the overall Sino-American relationship. American officials such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio have employed “strategic stability” in this broader sense. But the full term, “constructive strategic stability,” was apparently first used by Xi Jinping and other Chinese leaders. They defined a relationship marked by cooperation as the foundation, with moderate competition, manageable differences, and a durable peace. The American side then accepted the full term (not necessarily China’s definition), adding “…on the basis of fairness and reciprocity.”The Chinese origin and definition of constructive strategic stability might make some observers cautious, but that is not a reason to reject it. The test should be whether Washington defines the term and accepts it in ways that protect and advance American interests and constrain dangerous behavior on both sides. Washington should resist any definition equating the concept to one-sided respect for Beijing’s red lines.As I use the term, constructive strategic stability denotes both a political process and an outcome: a stable, mutually advantageous relationship and orientation to the international order. It assumes that neither the United States nor China is an existential threat to the other in every day-to-day circumstance outside the extreme case of a nuclear war, nor on a path to inevitable decline or dominance of one over the other. It recognizes that both, through their interaction, create dangerous, virtually unbounded competition. And it posits that global and national order and prosperity require extensive bilateral cooperation and mutual benefit, which necessitate substantive accommodation and reciprocal restraint.Some level of rivalry and competition are unavoidable, given the two powers’ contrasting political systems and search for security and prosperity amid scarce resources. Nonetheless, Beijing and Washington should not allow rivalry to overshadow the obvious need to create lasting stability in their relationship and address those major, sometimes existential threats demanding cooperation, including climate warming, pandemics, AI governance, global financial stability, and nuclear

sources.headline: Can the China-US Detente Last?
sources.text:
The recent thaw in China-U.S. relations – highlighted by reciprocal visits by President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping – raised the prospect of a more stable relationship between the world’s two largest powers. After years of escalating tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic mistrust, both governments appear willing to step back from the brink. The emerging language of “constructive strategic stability” suggests that Washington and Beijing may be converging on the need to manage their rivalry rather than allow it to define every aspect of their relationship.
But agreement on the need to manage competition is not the same as agreement on its terms. The two sides may have reached a shared conclusion that escalation is too costly without resolving the underlying disputes that drove them toward confrontation in the first place. If so, the current detente could prove less a turning point than a temporary adjustment in a much longer strategic contest.
The history of Soviet-U.S. detente offers a useful way to understand this possibility – not because the China-U.S. relationship is destined to follow the same trajectory, but because it highlights a central problem of great power relations: the conditions that encourage rivals to seek restraint may also make that restraint difficult to sustain.
Why Now?
The current thaw cannot be understood in isolation. It is the latest stage in more than a decade of intensifying strategic competition between China and the United States.
The Obama administration’s “Pivot to Asia” signaled a stronger U.S. commitment to the region as China’s power grew. Washington presented its policy as an effort to sustain regional order, while Beijing increasingly viewed U.S. initiatives through the lens of strategic containment. Yet competition remained partly bounded by the hope that economic interdependence and diplomatic engagement could prevent rivalry from overwhelming the relationship.
The first Trump administration marked a more decisive turn. The 2018 trade war transformed economic grievances into a central instrument of strategic competition. The Biden administration subsequently retained much of the competitive framework while expanding restrictions in areas such as advanced technology. Across successive administrations, Washington’s approach increasingly treated China not simply as a difficult partner but as a long-term strategic competitor.
The escalation of 2025-26 exposed the limits of this approach. Tariffs and countermeasures, particularly China’s leverage over rare earths and other critical supply chains, demonstrated that both countries possess vulnerabilities the other can exploit. But the ability to impose costs does not necessarily translate into a sustainable strategic advantage. Escalation can inflict damage on the opponent while simultaneously disrupting domestic industries, unsettling markets, and narrowing the room for diplomatic maneuver.
This gave both governments incentives to pursue a pause. Washington wants to stabilize trade, reduce supply chain exposure, and avoid a prolonged confrontation that complicates its broader economic and strategic priorities. Beijing has reasons to ease external pressure, preserve access to important markets and technologies, and secure a more predictable environment for economic development.
Their objectives for the detente, however, might not be identical. Washington may see a truce as an opportunity to rebuild leverage and reduce dependence on Chinese inputs. Beijing may see it as an opportunity to protect its economic position, limit U.S. pressure, and consolidate gains made during the confrontation. Each side can welcome stability while preparing for the possibility that competition will intensify again.
The significance of “constructive strategic stability” therefore lies less in whether it signals a fundamental reconciliation than in what the two governments understand it to mean. Does stability imply shared limits on competition, or merely a shared interest in preventing competition from becoming unmanageable? The distinction will determine whether the current thaw can endure.
What Detente Can – and Cannot – Do
The Soviet-U.S. experience is instructive in this regard. During the Cold War, detente emerged not because Washington and Moscow overcame their ideological rivalry, but because both recognized the dangers and costs of unconstrained confrontation. Arms control negotiations and diplomatic engagement could reduce the risks of escalation even while the two superpowers continued to compete for strategic advantage.
Yet detente never eliminated the underlying sources of rivalry. Disputes over regional conflicts, military competition, and divergent conceptions of international order repeatedly strained the Soviet-U.S. relationship. Changes in strategic calculations and domestic political environments also affected the willingness of leaders to sustain restraint. Detente could manage competition, but it could not make incompatible interests disappear.
The lesson for Washington and Beijing is not that their relationship will inevitably reproduce the Soviet-U.S. trajectory. Their economic interdependence, technological competition, and regional strategic dynamics differ substantially from those of the Cold War. Rather, the historical comparison directs attention to the conditions under which detente becomes self-reinforcing – or begins to unravel.
First, relative power matters. If either side believes that time is working decisively in its favor, it may view restraint as an unnecessary concession. Conversely, if leaders conclude that neither side can impose its will without incurring prohibitive costs, compromise may become more attractive. But a temporary balance of leverage can be unstable, especially when both governments are racing to reduce their dependence on the other.
Second, detente is vulnerable to miscalculation. Measures intended as defensive preparations may be interpreted as offensive moves, prompting countermeasures that gradually erode trust. Washington’s efforts to diversify critical supply chains and strengthen technological resilience may reduce its exposure to Chinese coercion. Beijing’s efforts to insulate itself from American economic pressure may serve a similar purpose. Such measures can make future crises less costly to withstand, but they can also weaken the mutual vulnerabilities that currently encourage restraint.
Third, domestic politics can narrow the space for compromise. Leaders must defend their policies against critics who regard accommodation as weakness or believe that strategic competition requires sustained pressure. Electoral cycles, economic pressures, and leadership changes can alter the political value of engagement. Even when leaders reach an informal understanding, they may struggle to preserve it if their domestic coalitions interpret restraint differently.
These dynamics suggest that detente is not simply a one-time choice between confrontation and cooperation. It is an ongoing contest over the boundaries of acceptable competition.
From a Pause to a Durable Arrangement?
The central question is therefore not whether the current China-U.S. detente will last, but what would make it more resilient.
One indicator is whether diplomatic engagement produces mechanisms that can survive political shocks. Regular communication, crisis-management procedures, and clear expectations about military interactions would matter more than the symbolism of leader-level meetings alone.
Another sign is whether both sides develop a more consistent understanding of the limits of competition. They need not agree on the ultimate distribution of power, but they must have some shared sense of which actions risk turning rivalry into a crisis.
A third indicator is how each government uses the breathing room created by detente. If restraint primarily enables both sides to prepare for a more intense confrontation, the thaw may postpone rather than resolve the next crisis. If it creates incentives to preserve communication, contain disputes, and cooperate where interests overlap, it may gradually acquire a more durable foundation.
Washington and Beijing may be learning that neither can easily defeat the other without paying an unacceptable price. But recognizing the costs of escalation is only the beginning of strategic stability. Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition. The same reduction in tensions that makes diplomacy possible can also give both sides time to reduce their vulnerabilities and reassess their strategic positions. That is the paradox of the current moment.
The immediate thaw should therefore be welcomed without being mistaken for a permanent settlement. The ultimate significance will depend on whether the two powers use restraint to establish more predictable rules for managing rivalry – or simply to prepare for the next round of confrontation.

sources.headline: What the US and China Should Discuss at APEC
sources.text:
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations.
In the September summit, already their second of 2026, one key area stood out as the focus: artificial intelligence. The risks of AI now have a dedicated channel for discussion. There’s not yet a corresponding China-U.S. platform for talking about the economics of the AI race.
During Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May, the two leaders agreed to restart government-to-government AI dialogue. In September, at the eighth round of economic consultations in New York and Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first AI dialogue within that framework. They agreed to establish a channel for communications on AI incidents, and scheduled a second round of talks before the end of November.
Shortly thereafter, at the presidential summit, Xi described China and the United States as two AI powers that should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other.” He added, “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.” Trump noted that discussions on “pressing issues” related to (among other topics) AI, which he calls “superintelligence,” could “promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” Both leaders thus offered the new dialogue platform political cover.
That is genuine progress, with a revealing limit. All the steps thus far – the exchanges on risks and benefits, the incident channel, the push for lab self-regulation – concern the dangers AI might create. Nothing yet addresses the looming economic problem of the AI sector.
The Growing AI Bubble
In the United States, recent developments are rather worrying. The business model for U.S. frontier AI businesses assumes that compute demand will keep growing exponentially, model capability will convert reliably into revenue, and capital will stay patient. All three assumptions are looking increasingly risky.
The capex needed to remain at the frontier is heavier, relative to the industry’s age, than anything technology has carried before. Utilities are signing power contracts for gigawatts of capacity that do not exist.
Meanwhile, Wall Street has started asking a question it ignored a year ago: where, exactly, is the return? In July, efficient Chinese open-weight models showed that frontier-level performance could be reached with a fraction of the compute. AI-linked U.S. equities sold off hard; analysts stepped back from price targets built on the assumption of permanent scarcity.
China has the mirror-image problem. Chinese companies are trying to close the frontier gap under foreign constraints while having to produce returns large enough to justify the spending at home. In a September study, the Rhodium Group calculated that the combined free cash flow of Chinese tech giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu swung from positive 170 billion yuan in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026.
The five American hyperscalers saw their own fall from $191 billion to $14 billion and raised $163 billion in long-term debt in six months to keep building.
Clearly, neither the U.S. nor the Chinese AI sector can fund this race from operations anymore. Both countries’ capital markets are tired of narratives without actual returns. Patience on both sides is wearing thin.
The China-U.S. competition exacerbates these economic dynamics. Each new round of U.S. export controls accelerates the Chinese substitution process, which shrinks the market available for American firms. At the same time, deeper substitution raises the investment China must absorb, which worsens China’s return-on-capital problem.
In other words, further escalation in the AI race might drain away the capital both systems depends on. This is not a moral argument, but a real financial dilemma.
Washington and Beijing have already conceded, in their September dialogue, that they face some common risks from AI risks. What’s not clear is whether the economic problem is included on that agenda.
The Chance at Shenzhen
The November APEC summit offers an unusually practical setting for addressing this issue. The APEC CEO Summit will bring about 1,000 business leaders to Shenzhen with AI on the formal agenda and a Shenzhen Initiative to be released. The host city itself, long nicknamed the Silicon Valley of the East, holds China’s densest cluster of AI and robotics firms.
Unofficial channels are also in place. Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy and the Brookings Institution have hosted 14 rounds of China-U.S. AI dialogue since 2019, with Microsoft’s former chief research and strategy officer Craig Mundie serving as a co-chair.
Three deliverables should be on the agenda for the APEC meeting.
First, China and the United States should add the missing piece of the puzzle in Shenzhen. The official AI dialogue will be held in November; at the APEC summit, both sides can start a standing China-U.S. AI economics dialogue mechanism supported by think tanks and industry associations, the “track two” format long used in China-U.S. exchanges.
Every official AI conversation so far lacks the people who control the money: finance officials, stock market regulators, and executives. The first such dialogue could take place on the margins of the APEC meeting, convened by think tanks and industry associations rather than ministries.
In Shenzhen, the Guangdong Artificial Intelligence Industry Association – which operates the Guangdong AI & Robotics Overseas Service Center, the province’s platform for firms going global – could co-convene, alongside established think tanks, a working session between U.S. investors, analysts, and executives and their Guangdong counterparts, on the industry’s own ground.
Why start with the “track two” format? Because the U.S. and Chinese governments would find it hard to host this conversation. No U.S. administration can openly entertain the thought that its AI boom may be overextended; no Chinese ministry can candidly compare burn rates with a foreign power. Finance officials can talk to economists, and economists can talk to each other. An unofficial venue is the only why this particular talk can happen.
Second, China and the United States should set a floor under export controls and market access in Shenzhen. Neither side can afford to be seen conducting negotiations over such fundamental issues, but they can quietly exchange red lines in a private setting. Misjudgment, not malice, triggers most crises. The cheapest deterrent is a sentence spoken early.
Third, it’s time to increase collaborations on the periphery. Standards for AI deployment in third countries – things like data governance, safety evaluation, labor displacement – don’t always pit U.S. and Chinese interests against each other. In fact, that happens far less often than either side assumes. Shenzhen has already hosted APEC-track discussions on responsible AI under the Policy Partnership on Science, Technology and Innovation framework. A joint signal from Washington and Beijing supporting shared regional norms would cost little, match the CEO Summit’s own agenda, and keep third parties from profiting from dueling standards.
Time Is Short
By greenlighting discussions on the economic side of AI, Washington would be shifting a burden, not making a concession. Industry leaders and academic would be the interlocutors, meaning the administration does not need to make more promises even while the Treasury gains more insight into AI’s financial stability.
For its part, Beijing would reinforce its longstanding claim that Chinese AI is an economic project rather than a military one. The talks would also give China’s capital-hungry sector a forum to argue against escalation using commercial – not diplomatic – logic.
The dialogue wouldn’t release a communiqué or joint statement. This would be a recurring conversation that, over time, builds a shared vocabulary for what sustainable AI competition could look like.
The capital markets are not waiting; they are repricing both countries’ AI sectors now. There’s still a chance for China and the U.S. to get ahead of the bubble, but the window is closing. After the U.S. midterms, coalition politics in Washington will harden, and every unmanaged month afterwards would strengthen the case for constraint in Beijing.
